# Native state/publication/recovery probe — plan before execution

Date: 2026-11-22, Europe/Kiev. Status: root and execution peer reviewed 2026-11-22; implementation approved; no native
PostgreSQL execution yet. This extends the prior native ALS/Yjs/browser evidence
with the actual state receiver and independently connected controllers.

## Boundary and reuse

Use a disposable real PostgreSQL **18.7** service (supported release published
2026-11-12), the released node-postgres driver with an exact verified pin, Node
24.22.3 and strict TypeScript 7.0.2. PostgreSQL 19.0 is newer; this deliberately
qualifies one supported 18.x profile, not every version. Record actual server
version/image identity and all installed package identities. No ORM, migration
framework, lock service, WAL or durable workflow engine is implemented.

The database adapter is a **test host's narrow authority fixture**, not a new
public library or replacement for an application's existing canonical store.
PostgreSQL owns transactions, uniqueness, row locks and crash rollback. One
checked-out client owns each transaction; no transaction uses pool.query.
Candidate/plugin code never executes inside these transactions.

The selected integration mode allows A's admitted computation/stream to finish
on A's retained implementation after B publishes, but fences new A commits to
shared mutable state. This is an explicit mode. It does not prescribe that all
long-lived operations lose write permission during every kind of update.

## Experimental seam

Publication/durable-attempt and shared-effect receiver are separate concerns:

- `readHead()` returns generation, monotonic publication revision, effect epoch
  and immutable cohort ID. These identities are separate; this strict-cutover
  fixture advances both revision and effect epoch on publication.
- `admitAttempt({attemptId, expectedRevision, expectedGeneration,
  targetGeneration, cohortDigest, baselineId})` durably records exact inputs.
  Reusing an ID with different inputs is rejected. Replaying the same inputs
  returns the existing attempt, including its selected baseline.
- `publishAttempt(attemptId)` uses the recorded expected head and returns a
  durable committed/conflict outcome in the same transaction as head mutation.
- `observeAttempt(attemptId)` returns recorded pending/committed/conflict or
  absent/unknown. An absent row is not evidence that external effects never ran.
- `guardedWrite({effectId, generation, effectEpoch, stateSchema, value})` checks the actual
  authority row and commits the effect under the same receiver transaction.
  Same key/different payload or authority is rejected. Replaying an already committed effect after cutover returns its original receipt without a new write; a new stale effect is rejected. The receiver rechecks the committed receipt after unique-key contention with a fresh statement snapshot.

Revisions and effect epochs cross the fixture boundary as decimal strings, not
lossy JS numbers. State schema, live generation, artifact/cohort and publication
revision are independent contract axes; a future compatible-write mode may
preserve an effect epoch across a code publication.
Cohort IDs are inert values supplied by the caller; no dependency grammar or
graph planner is recreated. Lock order: publication takes attempt then head; effects take head then effect. Publication serializes same-attempt callers before CAS; the second observes the original terminal result. No transaction path inverts these locks. Test-only synchronization hooks and raw clients are
kept out of these feature seams.

## Oracles and synchronization

Use explicit inter-process messages and database-visible lock waits
(`pg_blocking_pids`/`pg_stat_activity`) to establish ordering. A sleep is never
the only evidence that concurrent work started or was blocked. Every case has
a bounded timeout and finally cleanup of only its own clients/processes/schema.
No load/throughput conclusion is drawn from these schedules. The deliberately
held FOR SHARE lock is a test barrier; production SQL critical sections must be
bounded and contain no plugin callback or awaited Worker computation.

| ID | Decisive native case | Independent outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| S01 | Two connections capture the same expected head and race B versus C | Exactly one CAS publication succeeds; one conflicts; head revision advances once; both durable outcomes are coherent |
| S02 | Two connections concurrently submit the same attempt and publication | One durable attempt, one head advance, identical terminal outcome on replay |
| S03 | Same attempt ID with changed target, baseline or expected revision | Explicit mismatch; original immutable inputs/outcome remain unchanged |
| S04 | A1 → B1 → A2 distinct live generations, artifact/human label A reused; stale request from A1 | Monotonic publication revision and separate effect epoch reject stale publication/write despite repeated human/artifact label |
| S05 | Controller child commits publication, then exits before sending the application reply; fresh child/controller reconciles | Recorded outcome and head agree; same-attempt retry adds no publication/effect; claim is lost application reply, not a simulated lost PostgreSQL wire COMMIT acknowledgement or reconstructed Worker readiness |
| S06 | Controller child holds uncommitted head/outcome changes and is killed | Backend rollback leaves old head and no committed receipt; fresh controller can continue using the already recorded attempt |
| S07 | Negative control: old writer uses FOR KEY SHARE on non-key head revision; B publishes before A commits | Actual late old write succeeds, demonstrating that this weaker lock is not the required fence |
| S08 | Positive control: old writer holds FOR SHARE through its state effect; B publisher contends | Native lock wait is observed; A commits before B publication; after B publishes, a new A write is rejected |
| S09 | A worker exits after a request was dispatched to the parent-owned sink; release that delayed request after B publishes | Guarded sink rejects stale A; separate explicitly unsafe sink accepts it, proving worker termination is not external-effect rollback |
| S10 | New writer stores a v2-only state variant; old decoder attempts read/write after code rollback | Actual old decoder rejects incompatible state; guarded rollback admission is denied; the expanded compatible writer profile remains readable by both |
| S11 | Durable attempt records baseline S0; controller dies; S1 appears; same attempt resumes | Resumed attempt retains S0; a genuinely new attempt may select S1 |
| S12 | Concurrent INSERT ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING + same-statement fallback SELECT encounters another uncommitted insert | Negative-control statement may return no row after the conflict commits; a fresh statement observes the winner; no missing receipt is mislabeled as absent authority |
| S13 | Artifact metadata deletion races a new retained-reference insertion with native FK restriction | No dangling committed canonical reference; identify which transaction succeeds. This does not prove physical object-store deletion or full runtime retention |

S09 is joint integration with the execution lane; it must use real Workers and
the real database effect sink, not only model counters. S10 uses explicit
consumer codecs and disposable JSONB state; a toy codec counterexample does not
qualify arbitrary production schema migrations.

## Evidence and scope

Preserve the pre-execution plan, exact sources/locks/configuration, installation
and strict-compiler logs, actual server identity, test output and machine-readable
observations, all failures and source hashes. Parent owns hosted workflow,
publication and immediate push. Native execution starts only after review.

Estimated fixture/integration code: 500–850 lines; tests/oracles/fault-child:
350–650 lines; research/configuration/evidence: 150–300 lines. No production code
is adopted. Design confidence 8/10, bounded achievable reliability 8/10,
complexity 6/10. These are planning judgments, not availability measurements.

Unqualified: PostgreSQL failover/power loss, distributed replica linearizability,
external network effects, generic workflow replay, every isolation level,
performance/overload bounds, arbitrary migration reversibility and production
library admission.

## Primary source basis already read

- PostgreSQL 18 explicit locking:
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/explicit-locking.html
- PostgreSQL 18 isolation/Read Committed:
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/transaction-iso.html
- PostgreSQL 18 INSERT/ON CONFLICT:
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-insert.html
- PostgreSQL 18.7 released version:
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/release-18-7.html
- node-postgres transaction ownership:
  https://node-postgres.com/features/transactions

Exact source/tag/package identities and additional industry counterexamples are
being recorded in sources.json; these documentation observations are not native
passes.

# Execution, resources and cohort probe plan

Status: proposed on 2026-11-22; no new runtime executed. Root review is required before implementing/running this bounded fixture. This plan adds evidence to Resources6/ALS5/SDK14; those results remain historical evidence, not new test counts.

## Question and selected policy

Can a prepared replacement execute an actual new TS implementation and dependency cohort, while an admitted operation retains its old cohort, and can we separately prove old execution has stopped and old writes are rejected?

Selected test policy: a request admitted to A may finish computation or a read/stream using A after B is published. Publication of B revokes A's authority to commit shared mutable state. This is an explicit policy choice; another host may drain all writes before publication. The adapter must not silently choose for the host.

## Existing mechanisms versus coordination

| Owner | Reused mechanism | Guarantee exercised | Does not provide |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Node | `Worker`, literal entry URL, ESM imports, `MessagePort`, `terminate()`/`exit` | Separate real execution contexts and module graphs; termination completion observable in parent | Publication, tenant authorization, database fencing, rollback of dispatched host effects |
| `@get-modular/resources` 0.2.2 | Public `createScope`, `resources.setup`, `control.close`, `CloseReport` | Own started acquisition, register cleanup, preserve late-acquisition custody, report cleanup debt | Borrower admission, graph/cohort selection, a process supervisor, physical-stop proof unless cleanup actually waits for it |
| State fixture | PostgreSQL transaction and narrow typed authority API | Commit/reconcile a selected cohort; receiver checks old effect authority | Executing/loading plugin code or restoring worker heap |
| Parent test | Explicit prepared A/B handles and barrier order | End-to-end composition of those mechanisms and independently asserted receipts | Production generation registry/kernel, dependency solver, generic RPC framework |

The published Resources README and archived Resources6 already show repeated `close()` retries only failed cleanup entries after a settled incomplete flight. We will verify the exact published implementation, then exercise debt with a real worker. A missing or different retry contract must remain visible debt, not be compensated with a custom retry loop masquerading as library behavior.

## Keep five identities separate

| Identity | Meaning and lifetime |
| --- | --- |
| `artifactDigest` | Hash of immutable entry and dependency bytes; two worker instances can run the same artifact |
| `cohortDigest` | Immutable set of artifact/dependency identities selected together; fixture computes a deterministic manifest hash, not a dependency resolver |
| `generationId` | One live worker instance; restart from the same artifact creates a new generation |
| `effectEpoch` | Authority under which an operation may commit a receiver-side mutation; distinct field even if this fixture initially advances it with publication |
| `revision` | PostgreSQL publication record concurrency token, encoded as an exact decimal string |

An operation captures its admitted generation, cohort and authority token once. Its later write must use that captured token, never refresh to the current head merely to pass the guard. An attempt ID identifies a publication retry; an effect ID identifies a mutation retry. Neither is a generation ID.

## Narrow fixture seams

State agent owns these experimental DB primitives (names may be finalized by that lane):

- `readHead()`.
- `admitAttempt({ attemptId, expectedRevision, expectedGeneration, targetGeneration, cohortDigest, baselineId })`: persist exact immutable inputs, reject same-ID/different-input reuse.
- `publishAttempt(attemptId)`: atomic head CAS and committed/conflict durable outcome; same-attempt replay returns the original outcome.
- `observeAttempt(attemptId)`: recorded pending/committed/conflict or unknown.
- `guardedWrite({ effectId, generation, effectEpoch, stateSchema, value })`: committed, stale, or same-effect replay. A committed effect replay after cutover returns the original receipt when exact inputs match. The operation's original authority is retained for the delayed parent-owned request.

Execution lane proposes one small fixture handle, kept outside any public production SPI:

- `prepareWorker({ generationId, artifact, scope })`: acquire a literal A/B worker in `resources.setup`; wait for its validated ready message, return the handle.
- `beginComputation({ operationId, admission })`: send a typed message to that exact worker; receive a first result and a parent-controlled continuation barrier.
- `continueComputation(operationId)`: receive final result from the same worker and dependency.
- `requestHostWrite({ operationId, effectId, admission, value })`: emit a message; the parent captures the original envelope and dispatches the DB operation after a separate test barrier.
- `close()` is the Resources scope operation; cleanup awaits `worker.terminate()` and observes `exit`. No homegrown stop receipt is issued before that event.

Transport is fixture-only structured data with validation at the `unknown` message boundary. No returned closure, cross-worker resource object, transferable state claim, or general RPC package is needed for this slice.

## Decisive scenarios

1. **Actual code and full cohort replacement.** A entry imports A dependency; B entry imports B dependency and uses different computation. Record source hashes. Pause admitted A between two dependency calls, publish B in PostgreSQL, start B work, resume A. Assert literal independent A/A and B/B outputs and immutable IDs, not just a changed configuration tag. No dynamic shared service lookup is used mid-operation.
2. **Irrevocable host request outlives guest.** A emits a host mutation envelope which the parent captures before termination. Publish B, close A and wait for native `exit`, then release the parent-owned request. Guarded receiver rejects A's exact stale token. An intentionally unguarded receiver negative control shows the already-dispatched host action can still commit after physical worker exit. Stopping the guest is not accepted as a write fence.
3. **Cancellation versus completed stop.** Observe native terminate Promise and exit order, and ensure no completion receipt appears merely from an abort request or abandoned close waiter. Do not rely on JavaScript `finally` executing inside a forcibly stopped worker.
4. **Cleanup debt has live consequences.** Inject one cleanup failure before actual `terminate`. A settled incomplete report must coexist with a still-live worker capable of answering a message. If published contract permits retry, a later `close` must actually terminate and clear only that debt; count distinct physical exits. This is additional proof beyond the prior listener-only debt test.
5. **Bound retention by physical ownership.** Exercise at most two simultaneously live worker generations under an explicit test policy. While A remains retained for a stream, B is active; admission of C is refused before acquiring another worker. After A's physical close, C can prepare. The oracle counts actual worker creation and exit receipts. No memory/RSS/GC leak bound or fleet policy is inferred.

Do not add another synthetic 250-listener loop, reimplement the previous late-file acquisition case, or claim database durability from an in-memory compare-and-swap.

## Build, running and review gates

- Maintained sources are ordinary strict `.ts`, compiler TypeScript >=7.0.2. Inspect exact resolved compiler and any tooling dependency before execution; no old embedded TS.
- Use root-approved Node >=24.18.0 and <25 (or supported >=26.10.0 <27) with exact version recorded. Pin Resources 0.2.2 and public tarball integrity; do not deep-import its source or private lifecycle-kernel.
- Emit normal JS using the declared compiler, then run Node's built-in test runner. No `tsx`/transpiler/compiler dependency introduced just for convenience.
- Separate deterministic local execution from hosted PostgreSQL integration. A locally passing worker test is not the DB E2E.
- Typecheck, tests, exact dependency lock, source manifest hashes, runtime identity and raw receipts are retained. The root decides hosted workflow ownership and archive assembly.
- Estimate: 5-7 `.ts` source files, about 300-450 maintained lines including fixture tests, no production runtime package. If adapters exceed this because RPC/admission machinery grows, reduce the fixture rather than invent infrastructure.

## Source-only work in parallel

Inspect and record current/pinned .NET collectible contexts and real reclamation failures; OSGi multi-reference binding semantics; OTP code-load/upgrade restrictions not already covered; Piscina worker-task contract; public Resources versus private lifecycle-kernel availability. Findings must state source-inspected, historically reported, proposed or executed. Native Effect remains its own typed scoped profile; no Promise adapter or new Effect execution is planned by this lane.

Reuse evaluation is narrow: Piscina's bounded-task pool, native Worker lifetime, and Comlink endpoint RPC are different responsibilities. Piscina abortable tasks do not share workers; an aborted task's rejection still precedes physical thread exit. Default sync atomics pauses detached async work between tasks. Comlink 4.4.2's public proxy release is not an awaitable drain/termination receipt; released-source and upstream fixes/issues must be distinguished. Do not install these alternatives collectively or build a custom RPC/supervisor to compensate.

## Explicit exclusions

No sandbox guarantee for Node Workers, no arbitrary ESM graph resolver, no coherent cohort guarantee across independent externally hot-swapped services, no heap restoration on restart, no arbitrary plugin cleanup guarantee, no native Effect execution evidence, no Wasm backend execution, no production-ready standalone library claim.

# Execution, resource ownership and dependency cohorts — deeper evidence

Date: 2026-11-22. Checkpoint before native execution. Source ledger: `sources.json`; concrete experimental plan: `PLAN.md`. Prior Resources6, ALS5 and SDK14 are not new results. This lane's new code has not yet run.

## Decisions changed or sharpened by this pass

1. **Use public Resources for custody, not as an admission mechanism.** Its published 0.2.2 source registers acquisition before invoking setup, waits for pending acquisitions on close, keeps failed cleanup as debt and retries only failed entries in the next close flight. No generation borrowing, routing or DB fencing follows from these APIs. The separate lifecycle-kernel remains `private: true` at Get Modular commit `33c032f8`; copying its state machine would create a second semantic owner. External publication/qualification or a deliberately narrower external contract is still needed before adopting that candidate. [EX-S01–03]
2. **Choose executor by work lifetime.** Native Worker plus Resources is the minimal honest mechanism for this long-lived generation probe. Piscina supplies an actual bounded-task queue, admission pressure, worker pooling and shutdown; default task completion pauses further asynchronous work until another task. That contract can fit CPU work, but a plugin service/stream does not become a bounded task because it runs in a pool. No Piscina/Comlink production dependency is selected by this research. [EX-S04–05]
3. **An RPC release is weaker than a stop receipt.** Comlink's latest release 4.4.2 exposes a synchronous proxy release, does not reject outstanding RPC promises on release, and contains a release-response bookkeeping bug fixed upstream after the release. Current source and released package must not be treated as the same artifact. [EX-S06–10]
4. **Full cohort affinity and resource retention need separate evidence.** A pinned service reference does not retain its underlying resource; retaining a worker does not prove that every external dynamic service call stays in the same cohort. The new fixture will hold an actual A operation while B is published, with distinct entry/dependency files, and separately observe actual worker exit. A parent-owned effect dispatched before exit is fenced at the DB receiver. [EX-S04, EX-S11–15; planned experiment]

## Reuse candidates and exclusion rules

| Candidate | Ready-made responsibility | Critical boundary | Recommendation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `@get-modular/resources` 0.2.2 | Started-acquisition custody; ordered finalizers; hierarchical scopes; close-flight and debt reports | No live borrower counting; cleanup completion is whatever the registered cleanup actually observes | Reuse through public root API. Register the owned executor as one resource; cleanup awaits its native stop receipt. |
| Native Node Worker 24.22.3 | Isolated JS execution context/module cache; messages; native async terminate/exit | No tenant sandbox, global memory isolation or external-effect rollback | Good first isolated TS execution profile, with narrow host capabilities and explicit artifact URLs. |
| Piscina released 5.3.2 | Worker pool, task queue/backpressure, abortable tasks, `close`/`destroy` | Task result lifetime; abort rejects caller before physical exit; abortable tasks cannot share a worker | Use for bounded task workloads if measured need appears. Qualify close timeout and detached work before using for a generation owner. |
| Comlink released 4.4.2 | Typed remote object/endpoint ergonomics, structured clone/transfer | No operation admission, drain or supervisor; `releaseProxy` is not an awaitable stop | Possible transport adapter, with explicit in-flight ownership and stop settlement. Current release defects block assuming lifecycle completeness. |
| Private lifecycle-kernel candidate | Synchronous per-agent generation/call/custody bookkeeping | Private, instance-local tokens; no executor, callbacks, cleanup or durable authority | Resolve publication and consumer qualification with owner; do not deep-import or clone it. |

Piscina provenance check found a release/tag discrepancy: tag `v5.3.2` resolves to commit `6c7e5463`, whose source manifest says `5.3.1`; the separately downloaded npm tarball declares `5.3.2` and matches registry SHA-512 integrity. Both identities are retained. This is a reason to inspect the actual artifact, not evidence of malicious code. No package execution occurred.

## Actual failure mechanisms worth learning from

### Comlink: release, pending work and collection

At released commit `fd4b5266`, `releaseEndpoint` puts the release response resolver in a fresh map that the normal message listener does not consult. The public proxy release also clears the normal resolver map. Upstream commit `359584cc` (2025-01-13) fixes the map used for release and adds Node/browser regression tests for closing the returned MessagePort. It is later than the current latest release 4.4.2. [EX-S06–07]

Separately, issue #692 reports production calls hanging when a transient proxy is garbage collected during a suspended await; PR #693 proposes delaying endpoint release until outstanding requests drain and was still open at retrieval. Older issue #601 requests rejecting pending RPCs on explicit release. These are upstream reports plus source corroboration; this lane has not reproduced their GC schedules. [EX-S08–10]

**Our exclusion:** endpoint proxies remain strongly owned for the operation lifetime; releasing a proxy, cancelling a waiter, settling an RPC promise and stopping the executor are separate observations. Never rely on FinalizationRegistry to complete a correctness-critical transition. A failed endpoint must settle caller operations explicitly; pending promises cannot disappear from accounting just because a map was cleared.

### .NET: successful unload request does not prove unload

Collectible AssemblyLoadContext unload is cooperative: stacks, external strong roots, delegates, GC handles and even JIT-held temporaries can keep the context alive. Its unload event is a cleanup opportunity, not collection completion. The documented weak-reference/GC observation tests collection, while ordinary user resources still need their own release contract. [EX-S13]

The plugin tutorial also demonstrates a concrete contract-identity trap: copying `PluginBase.dll` into a plugin's private dependency directory can load a second interface identity, so the host no longer recognizes its implementation. Runtime support deliberately shares boundary assemblies while keeping private implementation dependencies separate. Its loader already resolves concurrent cache insertion races; recreating another cache would needlessly duplicate that mechanism. [EX-S14–15]

**Our inference:** a cohort manifest must distinguish immutable implementation dependencies from shared boundary/runtime contracts. Claiming full isolation while sharing mutable module singletons is invalid. A stop contract must say whether it observes request acceptance, execution exit, managed heap reclamation or OS-resource release; these are different adapter capabilities.

### Two shipped runtime fixes illustrate why ownership must be explicit

.NET 10.0.15 includes a NativeAOT EventPipe use-after-free fix: an effectively empty yield-while macro failed to wait for active writers. The upstream backport explicitly says intermittent failure, code review only. It is not a .NET plugin-update reproduction; it is a concrete instance of reclamation proceeding without the promised reader/writer barrier. [EX-S16]

The same release fixes NCrypt concurrent first-handle duplication: two threads could create independent holders for one native handle. The fix serializes the first ownership transition and adds a Windows concurrency test. The report links finalization exceptions capable of terminating the process. Subsequent ordinary parallel use was not the failing window. [EX-S17]

**Our exclusion:** a retention count or completed cancellation request is not proof that every physical user has finished. Ownership transfer must have one linearization point, especially at first acquisition and handoff. Do not clear debt or artifact references before the release operation's authoritative success condition.

## Cohort consistency: what established systems actually guarantee

OSGi Declarative Services gives each reference a static or dynamic policy. Dynamic bindings may change during component lifetime; static replacement deactivates/reactivates the consumer. These are dependency policies, not a promise of atomic replacement of several independently updated references. Bind failures can be logged while activation continues; deactivate/unbind failures are logged while teardown continues. Thus framework lifecycle state is not a sufficient readiness or cleanup-debt oracle for our stronger contract. [EX-S11]

OTP explicitly warns about dependencies between modules, processes and nodes, and about newly spawned processes executing old code between suspension and loading. Existing release machinery should be reused, but its local code operations cannot by themselves establish a whole-application cohort across independent actors. This sharpens, rather than repeats, the earlier two-code-version/purge notes. [EX-S12]

**Selected rule for our library:** an admitted operation captures one immutable cohort binding once. Cohort closure must cover the dependencies whose joint compatibility is required; external dynamic services need an explicit compatible protocol or their own retained binding. A mid-operation lookup of 'latest' is a visible opt-in policy, not the default. Get Modular remains the graph/digest owner; the fixture uses literal A/B manifests and does not implement a resolver.

## Planned native proof and remaining uncertainty

The reviewed plan uses real A/B Workers, actual different TS entry and dependency code, public Resources custody and the state lane's PostgreSQL authority. Five cases cover cohort retention, a delayed parent-owned stale write after native exit, precise terminate/exit ordering, responsive worker cleanup debt with public retry, and a two-live-worker retention budget. Physical exit will be asserted from Node's native event/Promise, never inferred from an AbortController that Worker does not accept. The joint test's strict-cutover policy lets A finish computation but rejects new A state commits after B publication.

Still source-only: OSGi, OTP, .NET, Piscina and Comlink; not all execution profiles or general arbitrary-plugin safety are qualified. Native Effect remains a native typed scoped profile, not a Promise wrapper. Production executor publication, portable ABI/cohort manifests, external resource brokers, process-tree termination, memory bounds and distributed/failover behavior remain separate work.

# Native editor update and late-result probe plan

Status: plan approved for installation, implementation and strict typecheck; native runtime awaits source review. Date: 2026-11-22.

Peer review: `/root/deep_state_protocol` approved this plan on 2026-11-22 with the incorporated precision requirements below. `/root` then approved installation, implementation and strict TypeScript 7.0.2 checking. A separate peer/root source review remains required before native runtime execution; root owns the hosted browser workflow.

## Decision this probe can change

Use native editor reconfiguration and history instead of creating a document/Undo subsystem in the plugin library. Determine the small contract still needed when an asynchronous contribution is replaced while its input text is unchanged. Qualify which editor state can survive an in-place contribution change or an explicit snapshot restore; do not equate either with a general plugin-state migration.

This is additional evidence beside the immutable React/Vite browser49 input and receipts. It does not rerun that fixture, implement another HMR protocol, qualify a production update orchestrator, or make CodeMirror mandatory for consumers.

## Read-only evidence already pinned

Published npm archives were read and SHA512-verified without installing or running them; exact archive/member hashes are in `source-provenance.json`.

| Package | Exact version | Published gitHead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@codemirror/state` | 6.7.6 | `651084c8a322b3a19b2bb3e00eee7d4a61d641af` |
| `@codemirror/view` | 6.43.15 | `da63d53a7b1f9011a09481f5fa2397294104d73a` |
| `@codemirror/commands` | 6.11.1 | `5d2ddbbf485a7e8b17c69cf58ebaebf8e375036c` |
| `@codemirror/lint` | 6.9.8 | `f71583124fa13052d0ac1c5ead5813448a429353` |

The registry now names `code.haverbeke.berlin` repositories. A GitHub default-branch read is therefore supplementary; released package bytes, not a presumed mirror branch, ground this experiment.

Two source-supported hypotheses deserve native negative controls:

1. Lint completion checks document object identity, but not the currently configured source identity. Reconfigure source A to B on the same document, complete B first and A later: A may overwrite B. `source/lint/index.js` has the exact `lintPlugin.run/update/destroy` implementation. This is not yet a reproduced released defect.
2. `historyField` JSON serializes changes, mappings and selections, but `HistEvent.fromJSON` restores an empty `effects` array. Document Undo may survive serialization while custom plugin effects in the same history event do not. This is a codec capability boundary, not presumed corruption or an upstream bug.

## Native test surface

Use direct CodeMirror `EditorView`, `Compartment.reconfigure`, `StateField`, `StateEffect`, native history/Undo/Redo, native `linter`, and public `setDiagnostics`/`forEachDiagnostic`. Use Playwright against a Vite-served page with real editable DOM, keyboard input, selection and rendered diagnostics. No React/CRDT wrapper, custom editor/history, monkey-patched internals, or invented reload transport.

Build tooling pins: TypeScript 7.0.2, Node 24.22.3, Vite 8.3.8, Playwright 1.65.1. All maintained fixture/test/config/runner source is `.ts`, `strict: true`; inspect the resolved compiler paths before execution. Exact transitive lock and browser/runtime inventory are recorded. Installation/typecheck/experiment execution require root and peer plan approval first.

## Scenarios and decisive observations

| ID | Native action | Evidence that would support the recommendation | Falsifier / failure handling |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CM-1 | Type a draft, establish native Undo and selection; replace a compartment containing a view contribution and the same state-field identity | Same editor DOM, draft, selection and history; new contribution handles the next interaction; old view plugin `destroy` observed | Record precise failed invariant; do not swap in a handwritten state restore to make it pass |
| CM-2 | Same-document native linter A starts, native linter B replaces it, resolve B then A | Native diagnostics may end at A, exposing a source-generation gap despite a current document | If native source identity already fences A, record protective behavior and remove unnecessary bridge |
| CM-3 | Native linter starts, edit document, resolve the old promise | Old-document diagnostics suppressed by CodeMirror's existing identity protection | Preserve this positive counterevidence; do not describe the native linter as generically unsafe |
| CM-4 | For explicitly managed contribution tasks, call public `setDiagnostics` only after checking the current contribution generation and host document revision at application time | Current result displayed; predecessor completion cannot replace it; completion for a changed document rejected | Gate lives in one small adapter; no new supervisor, authorization owner, editor scheduler or production guarantee |
| CM-5 | Start a task, edit and Undo back to identical text, then complete the original task | Monotonic document revision differs; original result rejected despite equal text | A text-content comparison alone must fail this negative control; no assertion that text equality implies same logical input |
| CM-6 | Remove native history extension in one transaction and re-add it in a second, without changing the document; compare explicit new-state reset | History clear preserves draft, selection and editor; document reset is reported separately and deliberately resets requested state | Do not use one transaction that removes then restores the same field and accidentally preserves history |
| CM-7 | Native edit carries text and a custom inverted state effect; compare direct Undo with `EditorState.toJSON/fromJSON` including `historyField` and a serializable custom field | Direct Undo reverses both; round-trip text/history may restore while custom inverse effect is absent | Report exact codec limitation and require application-owned migration/rebuild policy; do not serialize closures or claim full semantic Undo recovery |

CM-4/5 use trusted host-owned generation/revision values. They qualify stale-result prevention at a UI adapter boundary, not permission revocation or malicious plugin isolation. Cancellation can be requested for efficiency but never supplies the correctness proof. A disposal flag may additionally reject completions after the view owner is disposed; it does not prove all plugin resources were reclaimed.

The UI generation/revision tuple is separate from a durable state authority epoch. CM-2 uses explicit observed source-start and completion barriers for A and B, never timer guesses; any scheduled additional native invocation is recorded. CM-5 records native document object identity after Undo as well as equal text and a changed revision: it challenges a text-only guard, not CodeMirror's native identity guard. CM-7 checks custom field value restoration separately from inverse-effect restoration, both before and after Undo.

## Observability and user control

The fixture labels requested candidate, selected contribution, currently useful rendered result and rejection reason independently. A useful result identifies generation and document revision. Diagnostics from a predecessor are not relabelled as current. The report maps these observations into a consumer UI contract (preview dependency closure, pause/coalesce, version holds, reset/revert actions and resync) without making this fixture a second update authority.

Native OS IME is excluded from a synthetic composition-event claim. Source analysis covers composition-sensitive editor replacement; unless a real input path can be qualified separately, IME remains an explicit unqualified acceptance row.

## Expected artifacts and review boundary

- Exact lockfile, strict compiler output/version, native browser/runtime inventory and deterministic release schedule.
- One native fixture package; tests are grouped by the seven distinct scenarios, with every comparison reported under its scenario rather than called an independent end-to-end test.
- Raw JSON observations, browser trace/screenshots and original failure evidence if any. A corrective attempt receives a separate input identity and evidence directory.
- Narrow adapter code estimated at 25–60 LOC; fixture/UI 200–350 LOC; browser scenarios and strict tooling 200–350 LOC. Estimates exclude third-party source bytes and release work. No production package is delivered by this experiment.
- Engineering judgments: native reconfiguration reuse confidence 9/10, achievable reliability for the stated local UI boundary 8/10, integration complexity 3/10. Same-document lint-race hypothesis confidence 8/10 pending execution. General state migration and OS IME confidence remain unqualified.

Root owns tracked documents, workflow, remote execution, commits and immediate pushes. This lane only owns its isolated scratch directory. Peer must critique source-generation provenance, the equal-text/revision case, history codec interpretation and whether any control accidentally replaces the library mechanism before runtime execution.
